title: What Is Beautiful Is Good
text:
In 1972 Karen Dion, Ellen Berscheid and Elaine Walster of the University of Minnesota asked students to take part in what was presented as a study of how accurately people can judge others from photographs.

Each student received envelopes containing photos of three people of about college age, taken from yearbooks. Unknown to the participants, the faces had been chosen by other raters as clearly attractive, average or unattractive. For each face, the students rated personality traits such as kindness, sociability, sensitivity and strength of character. They also predicted what each person's life would be like: whether they would have a prestigious job, a happy marriage and a fulfilling social and professional life.

The attractive people were judged to have more socially desirable personalities across the board, and they were expected to have better jobs, happier marriages and more fulfilling lives. There was one interesting exception: attractive people were not expected to be better parents. The authors titled their paper with the stereotype they had uncovered: what is beautiful is good. Later research has confirmed this halo effect many times, and shown that it can influence decisions from hiring to court cases.
lesson: We all tend to credit good-looking people with good character. When judging someone for anything that matters, check whether a pleasant face is doing your thinking.
people: Karen Dion, Ellen Berscheid, Elaine Walster
source: Dion, K., Berscheid, E., and Walster, E. (1972). What is beautiful is good. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 24(3), 285-290.
